title: EvoLM: In Search of Lost Language Model Training Dynamics

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.1 (Training Setup) vs. Appendix B.2.3 (Training Data)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 2.1 states 'Continued Pre-training (CPT): Performed on FineMath [2]...' citing reference [2] (SmolLM2), but Appendix B.2.3 describes 'FineMath [38]: A curated dataset of mathematical texts...' citing reference [38], which is actually the FineWeb paper (Penedo et al.) already used for FineWeb-Edu earlier in the same appendix entry. The same dataset is attributed to two different, inconsistent references within the paper.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract / Introduction vs. Section 3.1 and Appendix A.1 (Table 4), Table 5
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract and introduction state the suite consists of '100+ decoder-only autoregressive LMs with 1B and 4B parameters,' and Section 2.1 says 'We initialize all models using the LLaMA-2 architecture with 1B and 4B parameters.' However, Section 3.1 explicitly trains and evaluates 0.5B models ('we pre-train 0.5B, 1B, and 4B models...'), and Table 4/Table 5 report full results and architecture details for 0.5B models, contradicting the stated model-size scope.

The text first argues that comparing 1B-320BT vs. 4B-80BT is 'misleading' because it ignores FLOPs/parameter-update differences ('The compute budget equivalence is thus misleading because training for more tokens on smaller models does not equate to the same compute expended on larger models with fewer tokens'), yet in the very next paragraph the paper uses this same comparison ('under a fixed pre-training compute budget (1B–320BT vs. 4B–80BT)') as valid evidence for Takeaway 2, directly contradicting its own methodological critique.

Takeaway 3 states that 'incorporating a small replay budget (e.g., 5%)' mitigates forgetting, but the best-performing configuration in Table 2 is '8BT FineWeb replay + 42BT FineMath' out of a 50BT total CPT budget, which is 8/50 = 16% replay, not 5%. The configurations closer to 5% (1.6/50 = 3.2%) actually underperformed.

Section 4.1 concludes 'these results caution against using such intermediate checkpoints as proxies for studying and understanding fully trained smaller models,' yet Section 2.1 explicitly states 'models are analyzed using both final checkpoints and representative intermediate checkpoints throughout training,' and Section 3's scaling studies rely on such checkpoints across token budgets, creating an internal methodological contradiction acknowledged in the text itself ('This conflicting usage suggests a methodological inconsistency that undermines conclusions drawn from intermediate checkpoint analysis').

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.4 (Varying RL dataset size) vs. Takeaway 9
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 3.4 states that for RL dataset size, 'greedy, Maj@16, and RM@16 accuracies continue to increase from more data up to around 150–200K examples, after which gains flatten,' but Takeaway 9 claims 'saturation happens at 4–8 epochs or 50–100K examples in our study,' which directly conflicts with the 150-200K figure given in the body text.

Appendix A.3 states 'the Pearson correlation coefficients remain close to zero' for all upstream-downstream perplexity correlations, but Figure 13 reports r²=0.219 for the MATH dataset, implying r≈0.47, which is a moderate correlation, not 'close to zero' as claimed in the text.

The abstract/introduction claim the models 'achieve competitive performance... compared with other open-weight models with significantly more pretraining compute,' but Appendix A.1 explicitly states 'Table 4 compares EvoLM models to public baselines without harmonizing training hyperparameters or evaluation protocols... Thus, claims of state-of-the-art competitiveness should be tempered pending standardized, fair comparisons,' undermining the paper's own headline claim.

The Figure 1 discussion admits that 'notable run-to-run variability is not shown' and that 'confidence intervals would reveal considerable fluctuations... suggesting the apparent saturation may partly reflect noise rather than definitive plateauing,' yet Takeaway 1 confidently asserts 'excessive pre-training can lead not only to diminishing returns but also to degradation in downstream generalization,' treating the unverified plateau as an established fact despite the stated uncertainty.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.1 (Training Setup) vs. Section 3.2 / Table 2 / Figure 3
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 2.1 specifies that 'Continued Pre-training (CPT)...token budgets ranging from 2B to 42B,' but Section 3.2 states CPT tokens are varied 'from 0 (no CPT) to 50 BT,' and Table 2/Figure 3 include configurations such as 'FineMath 50BT' and replay mixes summing to 50BT, exceeding the stated 42B maximum.

Section 2.1 states pre-training budgets range 'from 20× model size (compute-optimal) to 320B tokens,' implying a per-model-size floor (e.g., 20BT for 1B, 80BT for 4B). However, Section 3.1 and Figure 1 apply a fixed absolute token-budget set {10BT, 20BT, 40BT, 80BT, 160BT, 320BT} uniformly across 0.5B, 1B, and 4B models, including budgets (e.g., 10BT, 20BT, 40BT for the 4B model) well below the stated 20× compute-optimal floor for larger models.
